samples.text:
Nowadays, many young people decide to take a year off after they finish school and before they start university. In my opinion, the advantages of this gap year are more than the disadvantages, although there are some problems too.

On the one hand, a gap year have several benefits. Firstly, students can work and save money for their studies. University is very expensive in many countries, so if a student work for one year, he can pay some of his fees and he will not need to borrow so much money. Secondly, a year off give them time to think about what they really want to study. Many students choose a subject quickly and later they regret about it. Also, travelling to other countries can make young people more independent and confident.

On the other hand, there are some disadvantages. The main problem is that some students lose their motivation to study. After one year of working or travelling, it can be difficult to go back to books and exams, and some of them never go to university at all. In addition, travelling abroad is costly, so only students from rich family can enjoy this kind of gap year. Another problem is that they will finish their degree one year later than their friends.

In conclusion, I believe that taking a year off between school and university is more positive than negative. Although some students may lose interest in studying, most of them can gain money, experience and a clearer idea about their future. Therefore, I think the advantages outweigh the disadvantages if the student plan the year carefully.

samples.text:
It has become increasingly common for school leavers to spend a year working, volunteering or travelling before they begin a university degree. While this break can create certain risks, I would argue that its benefits are considerably greater, provided that the year is used purposefully.

Admittedly, a year out of education has some clear drawbacks. Some students find it hard to return to academic study after a long break, since the habits of revision and concentration they built at school may fade. Others treat the year simply as an extended holiday, which achieves little beyond delaying their education and their entry into work. There is also a financial aspect: travelling abroad can be expensive, and students from less wealthy families may not be able to afford the kind of gap year that is often promoted in the media.

Despite this, the advantages are more significant. The most important is that a gap year allows young people to make a more informed choice about their future. At eighteen, many students select a course simply because of their exam results or pressure from parents, and some later drop out when they realise the subject does not suit them. Spending time in the workplace or doing voluntary work gives them a clearer picture about their strengths and interests. Moreover, experiences such as living away from home or managing a budget help them develop the maturity and independence that university life demands. A student who works locally for part of the year, for instance, can save money and gain useful experience without losing contact with learning.

In conclusion, although a gap year may reduce motivation for some and is not equally accessible to everyone, the chance to mature and choose a degree more carefully outweighs these disadvantages. The key is that the year should have a clear purpose rather than being time simply spent waiting.
samples.why: Clear position maintained throughout · both sides extended and supported, with some generalisation · logical organisation with a range of linkers · good collocation · mostly error-free with a minor preposition slip.

samples.text:
The practice of postponing university for a year, once associated mainly with affluent students travelling overseas, has become a mainstream option for school leavers. In my view, when the year is structured rather than aimless, the benefits it offers clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

Perhaps the strongest argument in favour of a gap year is that it leads to better-informed decisions about higher education. Students who move straight from school to university often commit to a three- or four-year course on the basis of limited self-knowledge, and a poor match between student and subject is a common reason for dropping out. A year spent in employment or volunteering exposes young people to the realities of working life, allowing them to test their interests before investing heavily in a degree. Equally valuable is the personal growth that comes from handling responsibilities outside the protective environment of school: someone who has held down a job, paid rent or organised their own travel is likely to arrive at university more self-reliant and more focused.

That said, the disadvantages should not be dismissed. A break of twelve months can erode study habits, and a minority of students never return to education at all, particularly if a job offers an immediate income that seems more attractive than further study. The year also postpones graduation and entry into a career, which carries a real cost in lost earnings. Furthermore, the more glamorous forms of gap year, such as extended travel abroad, remain out of reach for many families, which means the experience can reinforce existing inequalities.

On balance, however, most of these risks stem from poor planning rather than from the gap year itself. Where students set clear goals, combining paid work with volunteering or skills development, they tend to return to education with greater purpose.

Overall, therefore, I believe the advantages of a well-planned gap year outweigh its disadvantages, since the maturity and clarity it provides can shape the rest of a student's academic and professional life.
